# Transforming variables

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Transformations";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the blue whale is the [largest animal]{.hl} known to have lived. The biggest accurately measured one, a female, was 29.5 m long and weighed 180 tonnes.

_Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica; WWF_
:::

## Today

- Why we transform variables
- Linear transformations: units, centering, standardising
- Correlation: Pearson's r, and what it hides
- Logarithms: for predictors and for outcomes
- A note on the word "normalising"

## Last week

```{r}
tidy(m)[, 1:3]
```

. . .

Each extra gram of body mass goes with `r round(b1, 4)` mm more flipper, and a penguin of 0 g would have flippers `r round(b0, 1)` mm long.

. . .

The model is fine, but its numbers are awkward: a slope too small to picture, and an intercept that describes an impossible penguin. Today we fix both without touching the fit.

## Why transform?

| Goal | Example | Transformation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Coefficients that are easier to read | slope per kg, intercept for an average penguin | units, centering |
| Predictors on a common scale | body mass (g) against bill length (mm) | standardising |
| A shape the linear model can handle | skewed reaction times, word frequencies | logarithm |

. . .

The data stay the same. A transformation changes the scale on which we describe them.

## Linear vs non-linear {.smaller}

A [linear]{.hl} transformation adds, subtracts, multiplies or divides by a constant. A non-linear one, such as the logarithm, changes the shape of the distribution.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.0}
set.seed(3)
rt <- tibble(rt_ms = rlnorm(2000, meanlog = log(600), sdlog = 0.35))

bind_rows(
  tibble(scale = "Milliseconds",       value = rt$rt_ms),
  tibble(scale = "Seconds (÷ 1000)",   value = rt$rt_ms / 1000),
  tibble(scale = "z-score",            value = as.numeric(scale(rt$rt_ms))),
  tibble(scale = "log(milliseconds)",  value = log(rt$rt_ms))
) |>
  mutate(scale = fct_inorder(scale),
         type  = if_else(scale == "log(milliseconds)", "non-linear", "linear")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = type)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, colour = floor_col) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(linear = kingfisher, `non-linear` = hornbill)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", fill = NULL)
```

Simulated reaction times on four scales. The three linear ones are the same histogram with different numbers on the axis. Only the log changes the shape.

# Linear transformations

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` a nursing blue whale calf gains up to [90 kg]{.hl} a day: that is 3.75 kg an hour, or 0.09 tonnes a day. Same calf, different units.

_Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica_
:::

## Changing units

```{r}
pengs <- pengs |> mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)

coef(lm(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_g,  data = pengs))
coef(lm(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_kg, data = pengs))
```

. . .

Divide the predictor by 1000, and the slope is multiplied by 1000: `r round(b1 * 1000, 1)` mm per kilogram.

. . .

The line and its `R²` (`r round(r2, 2)`) stay the same; the numbers are just easier to read.

## Where is the intercept?

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
ggplot(pengs, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = b0, slope = b1, colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = moss) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = b0, colour = hornbill, size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 150, y = b0, hjust = 0, colour = hornbill, size = 5.5,
           label = paste("intercept =", round(b0, 1), "mm at 0 g")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 6500)) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```

The intercept is where the line crosses `x = 0`: far outside the data.

## Centering

Subtract the mean, so that 0 means "a penguin of average body mass":

```{r}
pengs <- pengs |>
  mutate(body_mass_c = body_mass_g - mean(body_mass_g))

coef(lm(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_c, data = pengs))
mean(pengs$flipper_length_mm)
```

. . .

The slope does not change. The intercept is now the mean flipper length: the predicted value for an average penguin.

## Centering

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
ggplot(pengs, aes(x = body_mass_c, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = moss) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = hornbill, fill = hornbill, linewidth = 1.4) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = mean(pengs$flipper_length_mm), colour = mist, size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g), centred: 0 = average", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```

The data and the line are unchanged, and only the `x` axis has moved. The intercept (white) sits in the middle of the data.

## Centre on any meaningful value {.smaller}

The mean is not the only choice. Subtract any value that makes 0 meaningful:

```{r}
pengs <- pengs |> mutate(body_mass_4kg = body_mass_g - 4000)
coef(lm(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_4kg, data = pengs))
```

. . .

The intercept is now the predicted flipper length of a 4 kg penguin.

. . .

In linguistic data:

| Centred predictor | The intercept describes |
|:--|:--|
| `age - 18` | an 18-year-old speaker |
| `year - 2000` | the year 2000 |
| `trial - 1` | the first trial |

## Standardising

A __z-score__: subtract the mean, then divide by the standard deviation.

<div class="formula">z = (x − mean) / SD</div>

```{r}
pengs <- pengs |>
  mutate(body_mass_z = (body_mass_g - mean(body_mass_g)) / sd(body_mass_g))

coef(lm(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_z, data = pengs))
```

. . .

The slope is now the change in flipper length for one standard deviation more body mass.

## What a z-score says

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.4}
mass_m <- mean(pengs$body_mass_g); mass_s <- sd(pengs$body_mass_g)
ggplot(pengs, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 150, fill = kingfisher, colour = floor_col, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mass_m + (-2:2) * mass_s, colour = hornbill, linetype = c("dotted", "dotted", "solid", "dotted", "dotted")) +
  annotate("label", x = mass_m + (-2:2) * mass_s, y = Inf, vjust = 1.3, label = paste("z =", -2:2),
           fill = floor_col, colour = hornbill, label.size = 0, size = 4.5) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Count")
```

A z-score says how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean: `z = 0` is average, `z = -2` is two SDs below it. From lecture 3, about 95% of values in a normal distribution lie between `z = -2` and `z = 2`.

## Comparing predictors {.smaller}

Which predicts flipper length more strongly: body mass (g) or bill length (mm)?

```{r}
c(coef(lm(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_g,    data = pengs))[2],
  coef(lm(flipper_length_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = pengs))[2])
```

. . .

Grams and millimetres cannot be compared. Standardise both. `scale()` computes z-scores, but returns a matrix, so wrap it in `as.numeric()`:

```{r}
pengs <- pengs |> mutate(bill_length_z = as.numeric(scale(bill_length_mm)))
c(coef(lm(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_z,   data = pengs))[2],
  coef(lm(flipper_length_mm ~ bill_length_z, data = pengs))[2])
```

. . .

Per standard deviation, body mass goes with a larger change in flipper length.

## Speaker normalisation

A classic linguistic use of z-scores: vowel formants.

. . .

Speakers with longer vocal tracts have lower formants overall. Raw F1 and F2 mix up which vowel and which speaker.

```{r}
set.seed(8)
vowel_means <- tribble(
  ~vowel, ~F1, ~F2,
  "i",    300, 2300,
  "a",    750, 1300,
  "u",    320,  800
)
formants <- crossing(speaker = c("A", "B"), vowel_means, token = 1:20) |>
  mutate(k  = if_else(speaker == "A", 1, 1.2),   # speaker B: shorter vocal tract
         F1 = F1 * k + rnorm(n(), 0, 40),
         F2 = F2 * k + rnorm(n(), 0, 120))
```

## Raw formants

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.6}
ggplot(formants, aes(x = F2, y = F1, colour = speaker, shape = vowel)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_reverse() + scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "F2 (Hz)", y = "F1 (Hz)", colour = "Speaker", shape = "Vowel") +
  guides(shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = mist)))
```

The same vowels from two speakers land in different places.

## Lobanov normalisation

z-score each formant within each speaker (Lobanov, 1971). With `.by` from lecture 2:

```{r}
formants_z <- formants |>
  mutate(across(c(F1, F2), \(x) as.numeric(scale(x))),
         .by = speaker)
```

. . .

`.by = speaker`: each speaker's F1 and F2 are z-scored using that speaker's own mean and SD.

## After normalisation

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.4}
ggplot(formants_z, aes(x = F2, y = F1, colour = speaker, shape = vowel)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_reverse() + scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "F2 (z, within speaker)", y = "F1 (z, within speaker)",
       colour = "Speaker", shape = "Vowel") +
  guides(shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = mist)))
```

After normalisation, the vowels overlap across speakers.

## Discussion

Lobanov normalisation removes the differences between speakers, so that vowels can be compared across them.

- When could those differences be exactly what you want to study?
- What would you lose by normalising in that case?

## Linear transformations: summary {.smaller}

```{r, echo = FALSE}
fit <- function(f) coef(lm(f, data = pengs))
tibble(
  predictor = c("body_mass_g", "body_mass_kg", "body_mass_c", "body_mass_4kg", "body_mass_z"),
  `0 means` = c("0 g", "0 kg", "average mass", "4 kg", "average mass"),
  intercept = c(fit(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_g)[1], fit(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_kg)[1],
                fit(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_c)[1], fit(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_4kg)[1],
                fit(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_z)[1]),
  slope     = c(fit(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_g)[2], fit(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_kg)[2],
                fit(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_c)[2], fit(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_4kg)[2],
                fit(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_z)[2]),
  `slope per` = c("1 g", "1 kg", "1 g", "1 g", "1 SD"),
  R2        = round(r2, 2)
) |>
  mutate(across(intercept:slope, \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

. . .

Linear transformations change what the numbers mean, while the fit stays the same.

# Correlation

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the heart of a blue whale that washed ashore in Newfoundland, Canada, in 2014 weighed about [180 kg]{.hl}. It is now on display at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto.

_Source: Royal Ontario Museum_
:::

## Pearson's r {.smaller}

The __correlation coefficient__ r measures how closely two variables follow a straight line.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.6}
set.seed(2)
make_r <- function(r, n = 150) {
  x <- rnorm(n); y <- r * x + sqrt(1 - r^2) * rnorm(n)
  tibble(x, y, label = paste("r =", r))
}
bind_rows(make_r(-0.8), make_r(0), make_r(0.4), make_r(0.9)) |>
  mutate(label = fct_inorder(label)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
```

- From -1 (perfect negative) through 0 (no linear relation) to +1 (perfect positive)
- It has no units: it is the same whether you measure in g, kg or tonnes

## `cor()` in R {.smaller}

```{r}
cor(penguins$flipper_length_mm, penguins$body_mass_g)
```

. . .

Missing values again. Use only complete pairs:

```{r}
cor(penguins$flipper_length_mm, penguins$body_mass_g, use = "complete.obs")
```

. . .

Per group, with `summarise()` and `.by`:

```{r}
pengs |> summarise(r = cor(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g), .by = species)
```

## Correlation and regression {.smaller}

Standardise both variables, and the regression slope is the correlation:

```{r}
pengs <- pengs |> mutate(flipper_z = as.numeric(scale(flipper_length_mm)))

coef(lm(flipper_z ~ body_mass_z, data = pengs))
cor(pengs$flipper_length_mm, pengs$body_mass_g)
```

. . .

And in simple regression, `R² = r²`:

```{r}
cor(pengs$flipper_length_mm, pengs$body_mass_g)^2
glance(m)$r.squared
```

## Same r, different data {.smaller}

Anscombe's quartet (1973), built into R as `anscombe`:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
quartet <- anscombe |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c(".value", "set"), names_pattern = "(.)(.)") |>
  mutate(set = paste("Data set", set))

quartet_r <- quartet |>
  summarise(r = cor(x, y), .by = set) |>
  mutate(label = paste("r =", round(r, 2)))

ggplot(quartet, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1, fullrange = TRUE) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = quartet_r, aes(x = 5, y = 12.5, label = label),
            colour = mist, hjust = 0, size = 5) +
  facet_wrap(~ set, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

Four data sets with the same means, the same regression line and the same correlation, __r = 0.82__. Only one of them looks like a straight-line relationship. Always plot first.

## Correlation by group {.smaller}

Bill length and bill depth, from last week's warning:

```{r}
bills <- drop_na(penguins, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)
cor(bills$bill_length_mm, bills$bill_depth_mm)
bills |> summarise(r = cor(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm), .by = species)
```

. . .

Negative overall, positive within every species: Simpson's paradox again. A correlation describes only the data you give it, and says nothing about the process behind them.

## Correlation is not causation

In children, shoe size and vocabulary size are correlated: children with bigger feet tend to know more words.

. . .

Bigger feet do not teach words. Both grow with a third variable: age.

. . .

A correlation, or a regression slope, tells us that two variables go together. Whether one causes the other is a question for the design of the study.

## Discussion

Suppose children who are read to at home every day know more words than children who are not.

- Does reading aloud cause vocabulary growth? What else could explain the correlation?
- What kind of study would let you decide?

# Logarithms

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` blue whale calls can reach [188 decibels]{.hl}. Decibels are a logarithmic scale: every 10 dB more means ten times the sound intensity.

_Source: WWF_
:::

## Magnitudes

Some linguistic variables span many orders of magnitude. Word frequency is the classic example:

```{r}
set.seed(5)
words <- tibble(rank = 1:2000,
                freq = round(1e6 / rank)) |>        # Zipf-like frequencies
  mutate(rt = exp(6.75 - 0.06 * log10(freq) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.18)))

range(words$freq)
```

. . .

The most frequent word is 2000 times more frequent than the least frequent one. `rt`: a simulated lexical decision time for each word, in ms.

## What is a logarithm? {.smaller}

A logarithm answers one question: how many times do I multiply the base by itself to get this number? `log10(1000)` is 3, because 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.

. . .

So the log turns multiplying into adding: each step of 1 on the log scale is one more multiplication by the base.

. . .

```{r}
log10(1000)        # 10^3 = 1000
log2(8)            # 2^3  = 8
log(exp(2))        # natural log, base e = 2.718...
exp(log(50))       # exp() undoes log()
```

## Which base?

| Function | Base | One unit means |
|---|---|---|
| `log10()` | 10 | a tenfold increase |
| `log2()` | 2 | a doubling |
| `log()` | e ≈ 2.718 | the default in R and in most models |

. . .

The base changes only the numbers on the axis, and the shape stays the same: `log10(x)` is just `log(x) / log(10)`. Choose the base that is easiest to explain.

## Zeros and negatives

```{r}
log(0)
log(-5)
```

. . .

The log is only defined for positive numbers.

. . .

Frequency counts often contain zeros (a word that never occurs in a corpus). A common fix is to add 1 first:

```{r}
log1p(c(0, 9, 99))     # same as log(c(0, 9, 99) + 1)
```

## Logging a predictor

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
bind_rows(
  mutate(words, x = freq,        scale = "Raw frequency"),
  mutate(words, x = log10(freq), scale = "log10(frequency)")
) |>
  mutate(scale = fct_inorder(scale)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = rt)) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.3, size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Reaction time (ms)")
```

On the raw scale, most words are squeezed against zero and a straight line fits badly. On the log scale, the relationship is close to linear.

## Logging a predictor

```{r}
m_freq <- lm(rt ~ log10(freq), data = words)
coef(m_freq)
```

. . .

Each tenfold increase in frequency (10 → 100 → 1000) goes with responses about `r round(-coef(m_freq)[2])` ms faster.

. . .

Frequency effects in language are usually [multiplicative]{.hl}: going from 10 to 100 matters about as much as going from 100,000 to 1,000,000.

## Logging the outcome {.smaller}

Reaction times are positive and [right-skewed]{.hl} (lecture 3). So are the residuals of a model fitted to raw RTs:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.8}
m_log <- lm(log(rt) ~ log10(freq), data = words)

bind_rows(
  tibble(model = "lm(rt ~ log10(freq))",      resid = as.numeric(scale(residuals(m_freq)))),
  tibble(model = "lm(log(rt) ~ log10(freq))", resid = as.numeric(scale(residuals(m_log))))
) |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = resid, fill = model)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, colour = floor_col) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(orchid, pandan)) +
  labs(x = "Residuals (z-scored)", y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

After the log, the residuals are much more symmetric: closer to what the linear model assumes (lecture 4).

## Reading a log outcome {.smaller}

```{r}
m_log <- lm(log(rt) ~ log10(freq), data = words)
coef(m_log)
exp(coef(m_log)[2])
```

. . .

On the log scale, effects multiply. Each tenfold increase in frequency multiplies the RT by `r round(exp(coef(m_log)[2]), 3)`: responses about `r round((1 - exp(coef(m_log)[2])) * 100, 1)`% faster.

. . .

Back to milliseconds with `exp()`:

```{r}
exp(predict(m_log, newdata = tibble(freq = c(10, 1000, 100000))))
```

## When to log

- The variable is positive and [right-skewed]{.hl}: RTs, durations, frequencies, counts
- Effects are plausibly [multiplicative]{.hl}: "x% faster" rather than "x ms faster"
- The residuals of the raw model are skewed or funnel-shaped

. . .

The log is not a cure-all. Report which variables you transformed and why, and interpret the coefficients on the transformed scale.

# The word "normalising"

## A slippery word {.smaller}

"Normalising" is used for several different operations:

| What people mean | What it does |
|:--|:--|
| [z-scoring]{.hl} | subtracts the mean and divides by the SD |
| min-max scaling | squeezes values into the range 0 to 1 |
| a normalising transformation | makes a distribution look more normal, e.g. a log |
| speaker normalisation | removes vocal tract differences in phonetics, e.g. Lobanov |

. . .

```{r}
x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)
(x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))     # min-max scaling
```

. . .

In your write-up, avoid the word on its own. Say exactly what you did: "F1 and F2 were z-scored within speaker (Lobanov, 1971)". See also Winter (2019), section 5.7.

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- __Units__ and __centering__ change what the intercept and slope mean; the fit stays the same
- __Standardising__ puts variables on a common scale: slopes per SD
- __Correlation__ is the slope between two z-scored variables: unitless, from −1 to 1
- The same r can come from very different data, so always plot
- __Logarithms__ turn multiplicative effects into additive ones, and tame skew
- Name your transformation precisely, instead of just writing "normalised"
:::
